newClaim.claimText: UQ Library advises coursework students to acknowledge AI use, including summarising, brainstorming, planning and editing. Assessment instructions and discipline-specific practices determine the required form and relevance of disclosure; students must check each task and course profile.

evidence.evidenceSnippet: You must acknowledge where you used AI in assessment, including where you have directly quoted or paraphrased AI-generated content or used tools to summarise readings, brainstorm ideas, plan your process, or for editing or proofreading purposes.
Your course profile will have guidance on how you should acknowledge any permitted use of AI in your assessments.

Expectations for disclosing, acknowledging or citing AI use are context-dependent. Assessment instructions should require disclosure only where it is relevant to the task and disciplinary practice and should state clearly what students need to provide.

newClaim.claimText: From Semester 2, 2026 UQ classifies assessment tasks as Secure or Open. Secure tasks specify approved materials and whether AI may be used; Open tasks permit resources including AI, subject to task instructions and any specified disclosure requirements. An 'AI required' condition applies to tasks assessing AI use.

evidence.evidenceSnippet: Assessment tasks are classified as secure or open,  with matching automated text added to course profiles to improve consistency and clarity. Task instructions must still specify the materials and tools students may use and any disclosure requirements.
From Semester 2 2026, this automated text replaced the requirement to manually add standard AI-use text to course profiles.

The assessment condition AI required has also been introduced and should be used when students are required to use AI and are assessed on their use of AI (e.g., tool selection, prompting, verification, and integration) within an assessment task.
Secure assessment instructions should identify the materials and tools students may use when completing the task, including whether AI use is allowed.
In open assessments, students may use resources such as notes, course materials and other tools, including AI, while completing the task.

newClaim.claimText: UQ provides Microsoft Copilot Chat at no additional cost to its staff and students through UQ Microsoft 365. This university-provided Copilot Chat is distinct from paid Microsoft 365 Copilot add-on licences. Access does not authorize AI use in every assessment. Age-based and Academic Title Holder restrictions recorded in an older staff page have not been reverified.

evidence.evidenceSnippet: As UQ's enterprise system, Copilot Chat provides a higher level of data security and privacy than other AI tools.
available to all UQ staff and students for no additional cost

UQ staff may have access through UQ organisational units.
	
Students may have access through personal accounts but it is not available via UQ.
UQ organisational units can purchase and manage Microsoft 365 Copilot licences for their staff. These add-on licences have a cost per staff member.
able to access information in manually uploaded files

newClaim.claimText: An appeal of a Misconduct Body penalty ordinarily suspends implementation, unless the body directs implementation despite appeal. A student may ask the Appeal Body chair to stay such a direction; the chair must consider that request urgently. The Appeal Body decision is final within UQ, after which a student may complain to the National Student Ombudsman; internal appeals should usually be exhausted first.

evidence.evidenceSnippet: The decision of an Appeal Body is final and there is no further recourse to further appeal within the University.
An appeal of the decision of a Misconduct Body under this Procedure suspends the implementation of any penalty imposed by the Misconduct Body that is the subject of the appeal.
Notwithstanding clause 80, a Misconduct Body may make a decision that the penalty is to be implemented despite any appeal (referred to in this section as an implementation direction).

Where the student remains dissatisfied with the outcome of an appeal process, the student may lodge a complaint with the National Student Ombudsman. The student misconduct appeal process within the University should usually be exhausted before a complaint is lodged with the Ombudsman.
A student may apply to the chairperson of the Appeal Body to stay an implementation direction, providing any supporting material the students wants the chairperson to consider.
The chairperson must consider urgently an application to stay an implementation direction, and will proceed in the way the chairperson decides.

newClaim.claimText: For a formal UQ student misconduct proceeding, the scheduled hearing follows at least 10 business days after the allegation notice and document bundle are provided to the student. An oral hearing occurs only if requested, and a student may bring a support person. A student is not entitled to a lawyer or representative unless the Misconduct Body chair gives prior written approval. The Body will endeavour to decide within 20 business days after the notice and bundle are provided; this is an endeavour, not a fixed deadline.

The student is not entitled to be represented by a lawyer or other representative at the hearing, except by prior written approval of the chairperson of the Misconduct Body.

newClaim.claimText: UQ Researcher Hub advises staff not to share sensitive or confidential research data with public AI tools and to assume deidentified data may be reidentified by public AI. UQ Copilot Chat suitability is described for SENSITIVE information without additional sensitivities; staff must still consider research agreements and approved storage locations.

evidence.evidenceSnippet: Avoid sharing sensitive or confidential information and data with public AI tools (i.e. non-enterprise tools).

Files uploaded as part of prompts are stored in the staff member’s OneDrive. This data will be retained in line with our M365 retention approaches. This may breach research agreements (e.g. if data can only be stored in UQRDM).
It has been assessed as suitable for UQ information classified as SENSITIVE (includes unpublished research data that doesn’t have additional sensitivities like health data).
Assume that deidentified data can be reidentified by public AI tools.

newClaim.claimText: ITSO describes Gemini Enterprise EDU access for both subscribed staff and students, including programme/course-sponsored student licences.

evidence.evidenceSnippet: Gemini Enterprise (EDU Edition) is a tailored, education-focused AI platform designed for universities, colleges, and schools. It provides campus-wide enterprise search, intelligent assistance, and workflow automation under strict educational data privacy (campus data is never used for model training) while utilizing a unified, pooled resource model to optimize campus-wide usage.

Student – Individual students can subscribe GE license for enhancing their learning experience. Please note certain academic programs or courses may provide or sponsor GE licenses for the students. Please visit this link for more details.
Staff – Departments or Schools interested subscribe GE for their staff members.  please contact cchelp@ust.hk for further subscription details.
Once you have secured your Google Gemini License, you can access it at https://gemini.ust.hk and sign-in with your HKUST account.

newClaim.claimText: HKUST ITSO publishes distinct campus generative-AI services with user-specific access and licensing, including Open WebUI, Gemini Enterprise EDU, Copilot Chat, paid Microsoft 365 Copilot and API access. Course use is separately governed by instructors.

evidence.evidenceSnippet: Open WebUI is a new platform provided by ITSO for supporting generative AI services. It provides a lot of enhanced features over the current HKUST GenAI platform and has the same level of chat data security protection.

Student – Individual students can subscribe GE license for enhancing their learning experience. Please note certain academic programs or courses may provide or sponsor GE licenses for the students. Please visit this link for more details.
Sign in to HKUST GenAI Platform (the Platform) at https://genai.ust.hk with a HKUST staff or student account.

For an additional subscription fee, HKUST staff can enable the fully licensed Microsoft 365 Copilot experience, which includes Microsoft Copilot Chat and priority access in AI performance and integration with Microsoft 365 apps.

HKUST Generative AI API is a unified, high-performance service hosted in the cloud that provides secure, scalable access to industry-leading AI models. Whether you are a developer, a researcher, a student, or a hobbyist, you can use API to explore the frontiers of AI and bring your ideas to life.

newClaim.claimText: U-M does not recommend the use of AI-detection technology given their high error rate. False positives and negatives are possible, and even likely.

evidence.evidenceSnippet: Language models generalize and summarize existing knowledge based on probability predictions of word sequences rather than copying it verbatim, and so it may be impossible to identify their use with certainty. While detection tools like Turnitin or GPTZero may report probability of AI authorship, they are easily circumvented and cannot provide definitive proof of cheating. False positives and negatives are possible, and even likely. U-M does not recommend the use of AI-detection technology at this time given their high error rate.

Detection tools are imperfect, and currently no software is able to detect AI-generated text with 100% certainty. AI detection tools can be used to identify situations where further inquiry into the use of AI-generated text may be needed. They should not be considered a definitive measure for cheating.

newClaim.claimText: U-M guidance gives instructors flexibility to allow or disallow GenAI by course and assessment, with clear syllabus and assignment expectations; course policies should align with applicable school or college misconduct policies.

evidence.evidenceSnippet: Instructors are disciplinary experts responsible for what is taught, appropriate pedagogies, and assessment methodologies. GenAI may influence all three, and as such, instructors need flexibility to allow or disallow the use of GenAI tools. If the latter policy is adopted, instructors should be aware that U-M does not currently support the use of surveillance and plagiarism detection tools as they cannot be reliably counted upon. Further, clear policies have to be formulated regarding punitive measures and how they may be enforced. If GenAI tools are allowed, the instructor should be clear which tools are allowed and in what capacity.

Teaching in the presence of ubiquitous GenAI tools should be considered a dynamic endeavor and necessitates flexibility. Approaches and expectations will vary by instructor, course, assessment, and activity. To ensure transparency, it is critical that expectations are clearly articulated in the syllabus and continually reinforced when assignments are given. Instructors should align their course policies with their college’s academic misconduct policies.

f the latter policy is adopted, instructors should be aware that U-M does not currently support the use of surveillance and plagiarism detection tools as they cannot be reliably counted upon. Further, clear policies have to be formulated regarding punitive measures and how they may be enforced. If GenAI tools are allowed, the instructor should be clear which tools are allowed and in what capacity.
It is also important to point out to students that although AI-generated content may appear reliable and factual, that is not always the case, and that inaccuracies, untruths, and false citations may be missed if one is overly reliant on the tools.
Syllabus Language
GenAI is changing rapidly, and n

ew tools will become available. Course policies therefore need to be provisional and subject to change. Several principles can guide instructors to develop course policies appropriate for their contexts:
Protect cognitive dimension of learning: GenAI should enhance, not hinder, learning.
Responsibility for content: Students are responsible for all content (ideas, facts, citations), however the work is generated. (Note: Chat GPT can generate untrue, biased, inaccurate, and hallucinatory content.)
Require ethical transparency: Students should be transparent about how they use GenAI and adhere to standards of academic integrity.
Explain academic misconduct: Instructors should distinguish betwee

n allowed and disallowed uses of GenAI, including how, when, and why GenAI may (not) be used.
Course policies might fall into one of three categories:
Specific uses of GenAI are encouraged (generating ideas, editing, translating, outlining)
Specific uses of GenAI are allowed if students clearly distinguish between their original work and GenAI output (highlighting output, tracking changes in GenAI output)
Any use of GenAI constitutes academic misconduct.

newClaim.claimText: An LSA student found responsible may submit a written appeal to the Academic Judiciary Committee within two weeks from the date of the resolution letter, challenging responsibility, the college sanction or both. Grounds include serious procedural error, significant previously unavailable evidence or excessive college sanctions. Sanctions remain during appeal. Discrimination/prohibited-behavior claims must also go to ECRT and pause appeal. AJC may reverse responsibility or recommend keeping, reducing or increasing sanctions.

evidence.evidenceSnippet:
A student who has been found responsible for academic misconduct may submit a written appeal to the LSA Academic Judiciary Committee (AJC), a committee composed of both undergraduate students and faculty members from the College of LSA.
Note: If students submit an appeal request, college- and course-level sanctions remain in place while it is pending. If an appeal is based on discrimination or other prohibited behavior, students must also file a report with the Equity, Civil Rights & Title IX Office (ECRT). The appeal process will pause until that matter is resolved.
Procedures
The student must submit an appeal within two weeks from the date of the resolution letter.
The appeal must state wh

at is being appealed: the finding of academic misconduct, the college sanction imposed, or both.
The appeal must also state and describe in detail at least one of the following grounds for appeal:
The procedure was violated in a way that seriously compromised the investigation and/or conclusions.
There is significant new evidence not reasonably available at the time of the meeting with the Coordinator of Academic Integrity or designee.
The college sanctions are excessive relative to the violation.
Appeals are not granted unless one or more of the above criteria are met and supported by evidence. 
Making a decision
A member of the AJC will decide whether the appeal has sufficient grounds to m

ove forward. If it does not, the appeal process ends and the Office of Student Academic Affairs' decision stands. There is no further appeal opportunity.
If it is determined that grounds for an appeal have been met, a panel of AJC members will review your case alongside evidence from the instructor and documentation of how the Office of Student Academic Affairs reached its decision.
After reviewing the appeal, the AJC may:
Reverse the finding of responsibility (overturn the original decision), or

newEvidence.evidenceSnippet:
A student who has been found responsible for academic misconduct may submit a written appeal to the LSA Academic Judiciary Committee (AJC), a committee composed of both undergraduate students and faculty members from the College of LSA.
Note: If students submit an appeal request, college- and course-level sanctions remain in place while it is pending. If an appeal is based on discrimination or other prohibited behavior, students must also file a report with the Equity, Civil Rights & Title IX Office (ECRT). The appeal process will pause until that matter is resolved.
Procedures
The student must submit an appeal within two weeks from the date of the resolution letter.
The appeal must state wh

at is being appealed: the finding of academic misconduct, the college sanction imposed, or both.
The appeal must also state and describe in detail at least one of the following grounds for appeal:
The procedure was violated in a way that seriously compromised the investigation and/or conclusions.
There is significant new evidence not reasonably available at the time of the meeting with the Coordinator of Academic Integrity or designee.
The college sanctions are excessive relative to the violation.
Appeals are not granted unless one or more of the above criteria are met and supported by evidence. 
Making a decision
A member of the AJC will decide whether the appeal has sufficient grounds to m

ove forward. If it does not, the appeal process ends and the Office of Student Academic Affairs' decision stands. There is no further appeal opportunity.
If it is determined that grounds for an appeal have been met, a panel of AJC members will review your case alongside evidence from the instructor and documentation of how the Office of Student Academic Affairs reached its decision.
After reviewing the appeal, the AJC may:
Reverse the finding of responsibility (overturn the original decision), or
Uphold the finding of responsibility. If it's upheld, the Committee may recommend that the Office of Student Affairs keep the sanction as is, reduce it, or increase it.
Students will be notified of
the outcome by email.

newClaim.claimText: In LSA SAA Resolution, the Coordinator of Academic Integrity or designee decides under the preponderance standard. Students receive allegations/evidence and may respond, present material and ask questions. Students should notify SAA when bringing a support person. The usual Honor Council participant does not advocate for or against the student.

evidence.evidenceSnippet:
What an SAA Resolution is
A faculty or staff member within LSA who believes academic misconduct has occurred may file a formal complaint of academic misconduct with the LSA Office of Student Academic Affairs who will determine if misconduct has occurred.
Important: The instructor should not impose any penalty or require remedial work until the case has been resolved. Once a case has been filed with the Office of Student Academic Affairs, it may not be withdrawn without the approval of the Assistant Dean. Barring unforeseen circumstances, cases will be resolved within the academic term (and typically within three weeks) in which the incident occurs.
SAA Resolution Procedures
Reporting academi

c misconduct
Instructor reports a possible case of academic misconduct to SAA using the Report of Suspected Misconduct form
Prior to the Academic Misconduct Meeting
SAA sends an email to the student stating that an instructor has reported what they believe to be a possible case of academic misconduct. The email also includes a link to set up an Academic Misconduct Meeting. 
Once an appointment is scheduled, SAA sends a confirmation email which contains evidence about the allegations of misconduct. 
The Academic Misconduct Meeting will determine whether the student is responsible, or not, for the alleged misconduct. An accused student should prepare for the Academic Misconduct Meeting by revi

ewing the information provided, asking any clarifying questions, and show up ready to present any of their own relevant information, read any statement, and/or ask further questions. 
During the Academic Misconduct Meeting
The Coordinator of Academic Integrity or designee will describe the allegations made, detail the supporting evidence, and review the range of college-level sanctions (e.g. disciplinary probation, suspension, or expulsion).
This is an opportunity for the student to be heard and to present their side of the incident. The student should be ready to present any relevant material, read a statement, and/or ask questions.
Typically, in each meeting a representative of the LSA Stu

dent Honor Council participates, though they do not advocate for or against the student.
Students should notify the Office of Student Academic Affairs if they will have a support person in attendance at the meeting.
In certain circumstances, the Coordinator of Academic Integrity may give the student the opportunity to ask questions of the accusing party, either by exchanging written questions or by asking questions during a subsequent meeting. This additional step will be completed prior to the Coordinator or designee’s final decision.
The meeting between the accused student and the Coordinator of Academic Integrity or designee may be virtual or in-person.
Making a decision
The Coordinator o

f Academic Integrity or designee determines whether a violation of the LSA Community Expectations of Academic Integrity has occurred and if the student is responsible for academic misconduct.
The standard of review is preponderance. This means that the student is not considered responsible unless the evidence demonstrates that it is "more likely than not" that academic misconduct has occurred.
The student will be informed by letter, with an email copy to the instructor(s), of the decision and sanction(s), if any, to be imposed.
If a student is found not responsible for academic misconduct, the instructor(s) will grade the student accordingly.

newClaim.claimText: In LSA, course-grade penalties follow the instructor’s syllabus/department policies; SAA may assign college sanctions including probation, reflective essay, suspension or expulsion. These are possible outcomes, not an automatic AI penalty.

evidence.evidenceSnippet:
If a student is found responsible for academic misconduct:
Course-level sanctions: appropriate grade penalties for the misconduct will be left up to the instructor based on syllabus grade policies or department policies, if applicable.
College-level sanctions: The student may be assigned college sanctions by the Office of Student Academic Affairs. Examples of these sanctions include: 
Disciplinary probation - students are placed on probation for one year. As part of this process, a notation is placed on the student's unofficial transcript. This notation serves as a warning and reprimand that the student has been found responsible for academic misconduct. After that one year period, the notat

ion is removed provided no further violations of academic misconduct have occurred.
Reflective Essay - the student must write an essay about their experience, share what they have learned from it, and discuss how they intend to incorporate LSA Community Expectations into their personal and academic life moving forward.
Suspension - the student is ineligible to enroll at the university for one semester and a permanent notation is added to their transcript. In order to re-enroll in future terms, the student must write a petition for reactivation at least two weeks prior to the start of the term they wish to enroll.
Expulsion - The student is permanently removed from the university.

newClaim.claimText: LSA instructors may use Instructor Resolution for non-egregious incidents meriting no consequence greater than zero on the assignment; remedial work may also apply. SAA Resolution is appropriate for possible course failure or more severe sanctions, previous responsibility findings, or falsified academic documents. While pending, students are presumed not responsible, may attend class, cannot drop/change grading option, and instructors may not impose penalties/remedial work. A pending end-of-term case may receive NR and prevents course credit/graduation.

evidence.evidenceSnippet:
An instructor within LSA who believes academic misconduct has occurred may choose either
Instructor Resolution: Resolve the matter directly with the student
Appropriate when: the incident is not egregious and merits no consequence greater than a zero on the assignment, though the student may be required to do additional, remedial work (e.g., rewrite a paper).
SAA Resolution: File a complaint to the Office of Student Academic Affairs, who will resolve the case. 
Appropriate when: the sanction may result in the student failing the course or more severe sanction, the student has a previous finding of responsibility, or the student is suspected of falsifying or misrepresenting academic documents

.
 
Examples of academic misconduct include, but are not limited to: cheating, plagiarism, inappropriate collaboration, falsification of data, records, or documents, and aiding and abetting dishonesty.
Deadlines: The complaint for any alleged instance of academic misconduct should be filed as soon as practical from the date of occurrence and should be submitted within 2 months of the date of the incident.
Privacy: Materials related to a formal complaint of academic misconduct or an instructor's report of a resolution will be maintained by the Office of Student Academic Affairs in compliance with the privacy expectations under the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act (FERPA).
While a mis

conduct case is pending, with either Instruction Resolution or SAA Resolution:
The student is presumed to not be responsible for the alleged misconduct and the student may continue to attend class and receive grades.
The instructor may NOT impose any penalty or require any remedial work until the case has been resolved.
The student may NOT change registration in the course (e.g. drop the course or change the grading option to Pass/Fail).
If the term ends and a final grade must be reported while a case is pending, the instructor should use the grade NR (No Report). NR is a temporary, neutral grade that may be used in special circumstances where a final grade is not yet able to be reported. Th

e student may not receive credit for the course in which the alleged misconduct occurred and may not graduate.
Note: Students found responsible for academic misconduct with either resolution are not eligible to drop or choose pass/fail grading for the course.

newClaim.claimText: U-M ITS AI data are not used for model training, but service input, prompt history, usage metadata and logs are processed, including sharing prompt data with cloud vendors. The notice does not establish a uniform retention period.

evidence.evidenceSnippet: Data shared with ITS AI Services by you will not be used to train the AI models made available by the U-M through the ITS AI Services.
Provide persistence of user prompt history across sessions with the ITS AI services.
We do not sell or license your personal information collected here. To operate the ITS AI Services, however, we must share your prompt data with the cloud vendor utilized to host the ITS AI services.
Crash reports and debugging logs

What Information We Collect
ITS AI Services collect your input into the AI applications when you directly provide it to us, such as when you log in, enter prompts or questions, and upload documents.
ITS AI Services also capture some information about you automatically when you use the services. Automatically collected information may include:
The Internet domain you use
Your device’s IP address
Your Internet Service Provider
Your Cell Phone Service Provider
The type of cell phone
The type of browser
The date and time of visit
The address of the website that linked to ITS AI Services
Information about your role at the U-M and other related HR and student data via Single Sign On.
Crash reports

and debugging logs
How We Use Personal Information
The University of Michigan uses information about your interactions with ITS AI Services to:
Monitor performance and make improvements to functionality and user experience.
Provide support for questions about using the web applications or troubleshoot issues.
Enforce token quota limitation and enable internal billing.
Provide persistence of user prompt history across sessions with the ITS AI services.
We use de-identified and/or aggregated information to:
Monitor trends on the use of the tool to inform the product roadmap.
Monitor application performance to inform improvements to the application, such as device and browser compatibility, ap

plication features, etc.
Develop projections for future usage and anticipate service costs.
The use of personal information collected by this service is safeguarded through several mechanisms, including Information Assurance and U-M policies, such as Privacy and the Need to Monitor and Access Records (SPG 601.11) and Institutional Data Stewardship Policy (SPG 601.12).
With Whom We Share Personal Information
We do not sell or license your personal information collected here. To operate the ITS AI Services, however, we must share your prompt data with the cloud vendor utilized to host the ITS AI services. 
Specifically, we share your information with Microsoft Azure Services and Google. Learn

more about Microsoft Azure’s privacy policy and Google's privacy policy.
We require U-M’s service providers to keep your personal information secure and do not allow them to use or share it for any purpose other than providing services on our behalf. 
In addition, you can choose to share your U-M Maizey experience with other U-M community members.
We may also share your personal information when required by law, or when we believe sharing will help to protect the safety, property, or rights of U-M, members of the U-M community, and U-M guests.

newClaim.claimText: U-M Google Gemini and Gemini Notebook (formerly NotebookLM) exclude sponsored affiliates, alumni and retirees; supported sensitive data vary by approved guide.

evidence.evidenceSnippet: Google Gemini is a generative AI chat and image generation app available to all University of Michigan faculty, staff, and students. (Sponsored affiliates, alumni, and retirees do not have access to Gemini.) Like U-M’s GenAI services, Gemini can be used to create new content, generate and edit images (using Nano Banana), help brainstorm ideas, draft or summarize writing, explore complex topics, and assist with research and creative work. You can connect and use some Google Workspace services within the Gemini web app.

Google Gemini Notebook (formerly NotebookLM) is an AI-powered research and note-taking assistant available to all University of Michigan faculty, staff, and students. (Sponsored affiliates, alumni, and retirees do not have access to Gemini Notebook.) Using Google's Gemini models, Gemini Notebook lets you upload your own sources, such as documents, PDFs, and Google Docs, and interact with them through summaries, questions, audio overviews, flashcards, AI-assisted exploration, and more. It is especially helpful for synthesizing large amounts of information across uploaded materials.

Google Gemini can be used for certain kinds of sensitive data, as detailed in the Sensitive Data Guide to IT Services.
You can access Gemini via the web app at https://gemini.google.com or mobile app (Android and iOS).
Learn more about Google Gemini features, access and support resources.

newClaim.claimText: OVPR internal peer-review guidance updated August 11, 2025 discourages generative AI reviewing and strongly discourages uploading other researchers’ grant proposals to commercial AI tools.

evidence.evidenceSnippet:
●​ The use of generative AI tools in peer review is discouraged. These tools struggle to
       assess novel and original ideas, may produce biased results, and have been shown to
       hallucinate.
    ●​ Secure AI platforms that are available through U-M ITS AI Services may complement the
       review process to address grammar, language, and writing clarity. If permitted by the
       funding agency (see below), certain AI tools may also be useful when analyzing data.
    ●​ Uploading, copying and pasting, or otherwise incorporating any part of another
       researcher’s grant application to a commercially available AI platform (e.g., chatGPT) is

●​ Uploading, copying and pasting, or otherwise incorporating any part of another
       researcher’s grant application to a commercially available AI platform (e.g., chatGPT) is
       strongly discouraged. Such platforms lack sufficient privacy protections and may utilize
       submitted information, whether through prompts or otherwise, to train the models used in

newClaim.claimText: ITS does not provide a campus-wide teaching/learning plagiarism checking system. Detector output can trigger inquiry but is not definitive proof, while iThenticate is described for researchers’ own work, not student evaluation.

evidence.evidenceSnippet: U-M does not currently provide a campus wide plagiarism checking system in the teaching and learning context. Use of these tools has not gained broad support on campus, thus the lack of a funded campus-wide offering. Typically, instructors engage students in education about plagiarism and use an honor code. In February 2024, the Office of the Vice President for Research (OVPR) announced that it had licensed the iThenticate tool for researchers to assess their own work for originality, but this tool is not to be used for evaluating student work. OVPR is working diligently to expand the University of Michigan's institutional license for iThenticate. Once all of the details are finalized, they
will share this important information broadly with the U-M research community.

newClaim.claimText: U-M sample syllabi allow instructors to specify GenAI disclosure, restrictions, or bans by activity, in alignment with college policy; examples are not automatically binding campus-wide rules.

evidence.evidenceSnippet:
Teaching in the presence of ubiquitous GenAI tools should be considered a dynamic endeavor and necessitates flexibility. Approaches and expectations will vary by instructor, course, assessment, and activity. To ensure transparency, it is critical that expectations are clearly articulated in the syllabus and continually reinforced when assignments are given. Instructors should align their course policies with their college’s academic misconduct policies.
Instructors are disciplinary experts responsible for what is taught, appropriate pedagogies, and assessment methodologies. GenAI may influence all three, and as such, instructors need flexibility to allow or disallow the use of GenAI tools. I

f the latter policy is adopted, instructors should be aware that U-M does not currently support the use of surveillance and plagiarism detection tools as they cannot be reliably counted upon. Further, clear policies have to be formulated regarding punitive measures and how they may be enforced. If GenAI tools are allowed, the instructor should be clear which tools are allowed and in what capacity.
It is also important to point out to students that although AI-generated content may appear reliable and factual, that is not always the case, and that inaccuracies, untruths, and false citations may be missed if one is overly reliant on the tools.
Syllabus Language
GenAI is changing rapidly, and n

ew tools will become available. Course policies therefore need to be provisional and subject to change. Several principles can guide instructors to develop course policies appropriate for their contexts:
Protect cognitive dimension of learning: GenAI should enhance, not hinder, learning.
Responsibility for content: Students are responsible for all content (ideas, facts, citations), however the work is generated. (Note: Chat GPT can generate untrue, biased, inaccurate, and hallucinatory content.)
Require ethical transparency: Students should be transparent about how they use GenAI and adhere to standards of academic integrity.
Explain academic misconduct: Instructors should distinguish betwee

n allowed and disallowed uses of GenAI, including how, when, and why GenAI may (not) be used.
Course policies might fall into one of three categories:
Specific uses of GenAI are encouraged (generating ideas, editing, translating, outlining)
Specific uses of GenAI are allowed if students clearly distinguish between their original work and GenAI output (highlighting output, tracking changes in GenAI output)
Any use of GenAI constitutes academic misconduct.
